This document accompanies the Snowflake Guide of the same name. It walks through:

- Connecting to the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data in `SNOWFLAKE_PUBLIC_DATA_FREE` with Ibis, using Workbench-managed Snowflake credentials
- Exploring that data with Posit Assistant, backed by a Snowflake Cortex model
- Building an interactive Shiny for Python dashboard over the same table
- Deploying the dashboard to Posit Connect so that it runs under each viewer's own Snowflake credentials

## Install the dependencies

Run this once in the terminal, in a virtual environment:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Connect to Snowflake data

`ibis.snowflake.connect()` picks up the Workbench-managed credentials through the
`workbench` entry in `connections.toml`, so no account, user, or password appears
in this file.

```{python}
import ibis

con = ibis.snowflake.connect(
    warehouse="DEFAULT_WH",
    database="SNOWFLAKE_PUBLIC_DATA_FREE",
    schema="PUBLIC_DATA_FREE",
    connection_name="workbench",
)

mortgage_data = con.table("HOME_MORTGAGE_DISCLOSURE_ATTRIBUTES")
mortgage_data.schema()
```

`mortgage_data` is a lazy table expression. Nothing has been pulled into Python
yet: Ibis translates each operation to SQL and Snowflake does the work.

```{python}
ibis.options.interactive = True

mortgage_data.select("YEAR", "STATE_NAME", "LOAN_TYPE", "LOAN_AMOUNT").head(10)
```

## Explore the data with Posit Assistant

This step is interactive, in the Posit Assistant pane rather than in a chunk.
Because Posit Assistant sees the variables in the live Python session, `con` and
`mortgage_data` above are already part of its context. Prompts to try:

```
Summarize the structure of the mortgage_data table
```

```
Explore the relationship between loan amounts and property types
```

```
How do loan approval rates vary across states? Push the work down to Snowflake.
```

```
Check mortgage_data for missing values and data quality issues
```

## A first aggregate

The dashboard's metrics are computed in the database, not in Python. This is the
same expression the app uses.

```{python}
(
    mortgage_data.filter(mortgage_data.STATE_NAME == "California")
    .aggregate(
        n=lambda t: t.count(),
        avg=lambda t: t.LOAN_AMOUNT.mean(),
        total=lambda t: t.LOAN_AMOUNT.sum(),
    )
)
```

To see the SQL Ibis generates:

```{python}
ibis.to_sql(
    mortgage_data.group_by("YEAR").aggregate(count=lambda t: t.count()).order_by("YEAR")
)
```

## Assemble the dashboard

The deployable app is `app.py` in this repository, reproduced below. It is not
executed here.

Two things about its shape are deliberate:

- All credential work happens inside `server()`. On Connect the viewer's token
  arrives as an HTTP header on the Shiny session, so it cannot be read at import
  time.
- Every filter and aggregation stays as an Ibis expression until a `to_pandas()`
  call at the last possible moment, so Snowflake does the scanning and grouping.
  The histogram is the exception, and it is explicitly bounded with `limit()`.

```python
{{< include app.py >}}
```

Run it locally with:

```bash
shiny run --reload app.py
```

## Deploy to Connect

Deploy from Positron with the Posit Publisher extension, including `app.py`,
`requirements.txt`, and `.python-version`, and attach the Snowflake integration.
The equivalent from the terminal registers the server once, then deploys:

```bash
python -m pip install "rsconnect-python[snowflake]"

rsconnect add \
  --server "https://connect/" \
  --name "spcs" \
  --api-key "your-connect-api-key" \
  --snowflake-connection-name "workbench"

rsconnect deploy shiny -n spcs --entrypoint app:app .
```

One step is not carried in the bundle: attach the Snowflake OAuth integration on
the **Runtime** tab of **Content Settings**, under **Integrations**. The
publisher's integration request only records a request; associating it is a
separate action in Connect. Attaching it also sets `SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT` on the
content, so no account identifier needs configuring by hand.

`.python-version` travels in the bundle and puts 3.12 in the generated manifest as
an explicit constraint, which Connect then matches.
